meta.title: French A0 → A2/B1 in a Year
meta.description: A self-paced, 364-day plan moving from zero French to solid A2 / early B1. Work through units in order, roughly one day of tasks at a time — it is fine to skip a day or repeat one; what matters is finishing each day's tasks before moving on.

dayTemplate.label: Grammar
dayTemplate.task: Read Grammar Focus 1 below. Copy out all the example sentences by hand, then write 5 new sentences of your own using the same pattern.

dayTemplate.label: Vocabulary
dayTemplate.task: Make flashcards (use the Flashcards tab) for this unit's vocabulary list. Drill until you can go through the whole deck without missing one. Then write 5 sentences, each using a different new word.

dayTemplate.label: Listening
dayTemplate.task: Open one of this unit's listening resources. Listen once for general meaning, then again while writing down 5 words or phrases you recognise.

dayTemplate.label: Grammar
dayTemplate.task: Read Grammar Focus 2 below. Say every example sentence out loud, then write 5 new sentences of your own using the same pattern.

dayTemplate.label: Reading
dayTemplate.task: Open one of this unit's reading resources. Read a short beginner-level text, underline unfamiliar words, and look up 10 of them.

dayTemplate.label: Pronunciation
dayTemplate.task: Read the Pronunciation Focus below. Practise the example words/sentences out loud 10 times each, ideally recording yourself to compare.

dayTemplate.label: Review
dayTemplate.task: Re-read both grammar focuses and skim your vocabulary flashcards. Write one short paragraph (3-4 sentences) combining this week's grammar and vocabulary.

dayTemplate.label: Grammar practice
dayTemplate.task: Go back over both grammar focuses. Write 8 more practice sentences that mix the two grammar points together with this unit's vocabulary.

dayTemplate.label: Writing
dayTemplate.task: Write a short journal entry or dialogue (6-8 sentences) using this unit's grammar and at least 8 vocabulary words.

dayTemplate.label: Listening
dayTemplate.task: Open the second listening resource for this unit. This time, try to summarise what you heard in 2-3 French sentences.

dayTemplate.label: Speaking
dayTemplate.task: Say this unit's example sentences and your own sentences out loud from memory (no reading). If possible, use a speaking-practice resource below to try a short real exchange.

dayTemplate.label: Reading
dayTemplate.task: Open the second reading resource for this unit. Read for detail this time, and write down the main idea in one French sentence.

dayTemplate.label: Full review
dayTemplate.task: Review everything from this unit: grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation. Redo any practice sentences you found hardest.

dayTemplate.label: Unit exam
dayTemplate.task: Take the Unit Exam (Quiz tab). Read every explanation, even for questions you got right, then note down anything you missed.

grammar.title: French pronunciation essentials
grammar.explanation: Most final consonants are silent, except C, R, F, L (remember "CaReFuL"). French has nasal vowels (an/en, on, in) made by pushing air through the nose without fully pronouncing the n. Liaison links a normally-silent final consonant to a vowel that starts the next word.

examples.en: pronounced "lez-ami" — liaison links the s to amis
the final t of "est" stays silent; "content" ends in a nasal sound

grammar.title: Être (to be) — present tense
grammar.explanation: Être is one of the two most important French verbs. It is irregular and must be memorised: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Use it for identity, nationality, profession and feelings.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels: an/en, on, in
pronunciation.tip: A nasal vowel sounds like the vowel pushed partly through the nose, with the n or m barely audible as a separate sound. Don't pronounce a hard English "n" at the end.

quiz.q: Which form of être matches "nous"?
quiz.explanation: Nous sommes is the correct pairing — each subject pronoun has its own être form.

quiz.q: Which final consonant is usually PRONOUNCED in French?
quiz.explanation: Remember "CaReFuL": C, R, F, L are the final consonants that are typically pronounced.

quiz.q: "Je suis étudiant" means:
quiz.explanation: Être + noun/adjective expresses identity or state — "I am a student."

quiz.q: Which word contains a nasal vowel?
quiz.explanation: "Bonjour" contains the nasal "on" sound.

quiz.q: What does "s'il vous plaît" mean?
quiz.explanation: S'il vous plaît is the formal/plural way to say "please"; s'il te plaît is informal.

quiz.q: Which subject pronoun pairs with "est"?
quiz.explanation: Il/elle/on est is the third-person singular form of être.

quiz.q: Liaison means:
options: Linking a silent final consonant to the next word's vowel sound
quiz.explanation: Liaison connects an otherwise-silent final consonant to a following vowel sound, as in "les amis."

quiz.q: How do you say "goodbye"?
quiz.explanation: Au revoir is the standard way to say goodbye.

grammar.title: Avoir (to have) — present tense
grammar.explanation: Avoir is the second essential irregular verb: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. French also uses avoir (not être) for age and some fixed expressions.

examples.en: I am twenty years old (literally "I have 20 years").

grammar.title: Negation with ne...pas
grammar.explanation: To negate a verb, wrap it in ne...pas (ne becomes n' before a vowel sound). Ne goes right before the conjugated verb, pas right after.

pronunciation.title: Adjective agreement changes pronunciation
pronunciation.tip: Many feminine adjectives add a final -e that makes a silent final consonant audible: "grand" (silent d) vs "grande" (d is pronounced).

examples.hint: grahn / grahnd — the d appears in the feminine

quiz.q: Which form of avoir matches "vous"?
quiz.explanation: Vous avez is the correct second-person plural/formal form of avoir.

quiz.q: How do you say "I am not tired"?
quiz.explanation: Ne goes directly before the conjugated verb and pas directly after: Je ne suis pas fatigué.

quiz.q: "J'ai vingt ans" uses which verb to express age?
quiz.explanation: French uses avoir, not être, to state age.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of "français"?
quiz.explanation: Most adjectives ending in -ais add -e for the feminine: française.

quiz.q: "Il n'a pas de chien" means:
quiz.explanation: Ne...pas negates avoir, and de replaces un/une after a negated verb.

quiz.q: Which adjective means "shy"?
quiz.explanation: Timide means shy.

quiz.q: Why is the d in "grande" pronounced but silent in "grand"?
options: The feminine -e makes the preceding consonant audible
It depends on the speaker's region
quiz.explanation: Adding the feminine -e reveals the consonant that is otherwise silent at the end of a word.

quiz.q: Which is the correct subject + avoir pairing?
quiz.explanation: Ils/elles ont is correct; the others mismatch subject and verb form.

grammar.title: Gender, articles and plurals
grammar.explanation: Every French noun is masculine or feminine; the article shows it: le/un (masc.), la/une (fem.), les/des (plural). Most nouns add -s for the plural (silent in speech). There is no reliable shortcut for gender — learn it with each word.

grammar.title: Regular -ER verbs in the present
grammar.explanation: The largest group of French verbs ends in -er (parler, aimer, habiter...). Drop -er and add: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

pronunciation.title: Silent -ent verb ending
pronunciation.tip: In -er verbs, the ils/elles form ending -ent is completely silent; it never sounds like "ent" in English.

quiz.q: What is the plural of "le livre"?
quiz.explanation: The article changes to les and the noun adds -s: les livres.

quiz.q: Which ending goes with "nous" for -er verbs?
quiz.explanation: Nous parlons — the nous form of -er verbs always ends in -ons.

quiz.q: How is the "ils/elles" -ent ending pronounced?
quiz.explanation: The -ent ending on -er verbs in the ils/elles form is silent.

quiz.q: "Une table" uses which type of article?
quiz.explanation: Une is the feminine indefinite article ("a/an").

quiz.q: Which verb form matches "tu"?
quiz.explanation: Tu parles is the correct second-person singular form.

quiz.q: "J'habite à Paris" means:
quiz.explanation: Habiter means "to live/reside".

quiz.q: Which word means "a pen"?
quiz.explanation: Un stylo is a pen.

quiz.q: How many grammatical genders does French have for nouns?
quiz.explanation: French nouns are either masculine or feminine — there is no neuter.

grammar.title: Possessive adjectives
grammar.explanation: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they describe, not with the owner: mon/ma/mes (my), ton/ta/tes (your, informal), son/sa/ses (his/her), notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs.

grammar.title: Asking questions
grammar.explanation: Three common ways to ask a question: rising intonation (Tu parles français?), adding est-ce que before a statement (Est-ce que tu parles français?), or inversion in formal speech (Parles-tu français?).

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu as une sœur ?

pronunciation.title: The French R
pronunciation.tip: The French R is made in the back of the throat (uvular), not rolled with the tongue tip like in Spanish. Practise gargling gently while saying "r".

quiz.q: Which possessive matches "ma sœur" if she were your brother instead?
quiz.explanation: Frère is masculine, so it takes mon, not ma — possessives agree with the noun's gender, not the owner's.

quiz.q: Which sentence is a formal inversion question?
options: Est-ce que tu as des enfants ?
quiz.explanation: As-tu...? inverts the verb and subject, which is the formal question pattern.

quiz.q: "Leur" means:
quiz.explanation: Leur/leurs is the possessive adjective for "their".

quiz.q: How is the French R typically produced?
options: In the back of the throat
quiz.explanation: The standard French R is a uvular sound made in the back of the throat.

quiz.q: What does "les enfants" mean?
quiz.explanation: Les enfants means "the children".

quiz.q: Which number is "cent"?
quiz.explanation: Cent means one hundred.

quiz.q: Possessive adjectives in French agree with:
quiz.explanation: Unlike English, French possessives agree with the gender/number of the noun being possessed.

quiz.q: Which starts a yes/no question without changing word order?
quiz.explanation: Est-ce que can be added before any statement to turn it into a question, with no word-order change.

units.title: Daily routine, reflexive verbs and -RE verbs

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs
grammar.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe actions you do to yourself and need a reflexive pronoun matching the subject: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive.

examples.fr: Je me lève à sept heures.

grammar.title: Regular -RE verbs in the present
grammar.explanation: Verbs ending in -re (attendre, vendre, répondre...) drop -re and add: -s, -s, nothing (for il/elle), -ons, -ez, -ent.

pronunciation.title: The French U vs OU sound
pronunciation.tip: French "u" (as in "tu") is a tight, rounded sound not found in English — round your lips as if saying "ee" but push them forward. "Ou" (as in "vous") is like English "oo".

examples.hint: rue (street, tight u) vs roue (wheel, oo)

quiz.q: Which reflexive pronoun matches "nous"?
quiz.explanation: Nous nous levons — the reflexive pronoun matches the subject pronoun.

quiz.q: "Je me lève" means:
quiz.explanation: Se lever means "to get (oneself) up".

quiz.q: What is the il/elle ending for -re verbs?
quiz.explanation: Il/elle attend — the third-person singular of -re verbs adds no extra letter.

quiz.q: Which sound is "tu"'s vowel closest to?
options: A tight rounded sound not in English
quiz.explanation: The French u is a distinct rounded-front vowel with no real English equivalent.

quiz.q: "J'attends le bus" means:
quiz.explanation: Attendre means "to wait for".

quiz.q: Which word means "evening"?
quiz.explanation: Le soir means "the evening".

quiz.q: Reflexive verbs are used when:
options: The subject and object of the action are the same person
quiz.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe an action the subject performs on themselves.

quiz.q: "Elle répond à la question" means:
quiz.explanation: Répondre means "to answer/respond".

grammar.title: Partitive articles: du, de la, des
grammar.explanation: Use du (masc.), de la (fem.), de l' (before a vowel) and des (plural) to say "some" of an uncountable or unspecified amount, especially with food and drink.

grammar.title: Aller and faire
grammar.explanation: Aller (to go) and faire (to do/make) are both irregular and extremely common. Aller: vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont. Faire: fais, fais, fait, faisons, faites, font.

pronunciation.title: The mute H and elision
pronunciation.tip: French h is always silent. Before most h-words and all vowel-starting words, le/la shorten to l' (elision) — le + eau → l'eau.

examples.hint: LOH — the h is silent, le becomes l'
leh-ari-KO — h silent, no elision here because this h is "aspirate"

quiz.q: Which partitive article goes with "eau" (feminine, starts with a vowel)?
quiz.explanation: De la shortens to de l' before a vowel sound: de l'eau.

quiz.q: Which verb form means "we are doing"?
quiz.explanation: Nous faisons is the first-person plural of faire.

quiz.q: "Je vais au marché" means:
quiz.explanation: Aller + à means "to go to".

quiz.q: Is the French letter H ever pronounced?
options: Only at the start of a word
quiz.explanation: The letter h is always silent in French, though some h's block elision/liaison ("aspirate h") while others don't.

quiz.q: What does "combien ça coûte ?" mean?
quiz.explanation: Combien ça coûte? asks for a price.

quiz.q: Which article is used for countable plural items like "some vegetables"?
quiz.explanation: Des légumes — des is the plural partitive/indefinite article.

quiz.q: Which is the correct faire form for "tu"?
quiz.explanation: Tu fais is the correct second-person singular form of faire.

quiz.q: "Pas cher" means:
quiz.explanation: Pas cher literally means "not expensive", i.e. cheap.

units.title: Talking about the past I: passé composé with avoir

grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir
grammar.explanation: The passé composé describes completed past actions. Most verbs form it with avoir + past participle. Regular participles: -er verbs → -é, -ir verbs → -i, -re verbs → -u.

grammar.title: Irregular past participles
grammar.explanation: Common irregular participles must be memorised individually: faire → fait, prendre → pris, voir → vu, être → été, avoir → eu, pouvoir → pu, vouloir → voulu.

pronunciation.title: Linking vowel sounds (enchaînement)
pronunciation.tip: Unlike liaison (silent letters), enchaînement links an already-pronounced final consonant smoothly to the next word's vowel, so phrases flow without gaps.

examples.hint: ell-ah-REEV — the l of elle flows into arrive

quiz.q: What is the past participle of "prendre"?
quiz.explanation: Prendre has the irregular participle pris.

quiz.q: Which auxiliary verb do most French verbs use in the passé composé?
quiz.explanation: Most verbs use avoir as the auxiliary in the passé composé.

quiz.q: "Nous avons fini le travail" means:
quiz.explanation: Avoir (present) + past participle = passé composé, a completed past action.

quiz.q: What is the regular participle ending for -ir verbs?
quiz.explanation: Regular -ir verbs form their participle with -i, e.g. fini.

quiz.q: What is the past participle of "être"?
quiz.explanation: Être's irregular past participle is été.

quiz.q: Enchaînement is different from liaison because:
options: It only happens with nasal vowels
It links a consonant that is already pronounced, not a silent one
quiz.explanation: Enchaînement links an already-sounded final consonant to the next vowel, unlike liaison which revives a silent one.

quiz.q: "Hier" means:
quiz.explanation: Hier means "yesterday".

quiz.q: Which sentence is correctly formed in the passé composé?
quiz.explanation: J'ai vu le film correctly uses avoir + the irregular participle vu.

units.title: Talking about the past II: passé composé with être

grammar.title: Passé composé with être
grammar.explanation: A small set of verbs of movement/state (often grouped under the mnemonic DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP: Devenir, Revenir, Monter, Rester, Sortir, Venir, Aller, Naître, Descendre, Entrer, Rentrer, Tomber, Retourner, Arriver, Mourir, Partir) use être instead of avoir.

grammar.title: Past participle agreement with être
grammar.explanation: With être, the past participle must agree in gender and number with the subject, just like an adjective: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for feminine plural.

examples.en: They (all feminine) went to the park.

pronunciation.title: Distinguishing é, è and e
pronunciation.tip: é is closed and sharp (like "ay"), è is open (like "eh" in "bed"), and an unaccented final e is often silent or very reduced.

quiz.q: Which verb takes être in the passé composé?
quiz.explanation: Partir is one of the "DR MRS VANDERTRAMP" verbs that use être.

quiz.q: "Elles sont allées au parc" — why does "allées" end in -ées?
options: Agreement with a feminine plural subject
All passé composé verbs end this way
quiz.explanation: With être, the participle agrees with the subject — here feminine plural, so -ées.

quiz.q: What does "naître" mean?
quiz.explanation: Naître means "to be born".

quiz.q: Does the past participle agree with the subject when avoir is the auxiliary (basic case)?
quiz.explanation: With avoir, the participle normally does not agree with the subject (there are object-pronoun exceptions learned later).

quiz.q: Which sound is "è" compared to "é"?
quiz.explanation: È is an open vowel sound, while é is closed.

quiz.q: "Nous sommes arrivés à midi" means:
quiz.explanation: Être (present) + participle = passé composé, a completed action in the past.

quiz.q: Which word means "a hobby"?
quiz.explanation: Un loisir means a hobby or leisure activity.

quiz.q: What is the feminine singular ending added to a past participle?
quiz.explanation: Feminine singular agreement adds -e to the participle.

units.title: Near future, weather and direct object pronouns

grammar.title: Futur proche: aller + infinitive
grammar.explanation: To talk about the near future or firm plans, conjugate aller in the present and add the infinitive of the main verb.

examples.en: They're going to travel in summer.

grammar.title: Direct object pronouns: le, la, les
grammar.explanation: Le (him/it, masc.), la (her/it, fem.) and les (them) replace a direct object noun and go right before the conjugated verb.

pronunciation.title: The French J and G(e/i) sound
pronunciation.tip: French j, and g before e/i, make a soft "zh" sound like the s in English "measure" — never like English j or hard g.

quiz.q: "Je vais manger" means:
quiz.explanation: Aller (present) + infinitive expresses the near future.

quiz.q: Which pronoun replaces a feminine singular direct object?
quiz.explanation: La replaces a feminine singular direct object.

quiz.q: Where does a direct object pronoun usually go?
options: At the end of the sentence
quiz.explanation: Object pronouns like le/la/les precede the conjugated verb in standard statements.

quiz.q: "Il pleut" means:
quiz.explanation: Il pleut means "it's raining".

quiz.q: How does French j sound?
quiz.explanation: French j is a soft "zh" sound, distinct from the hard English j.

quiz.q: Which season is "l'automne"?
quiz.explanation: L'automne means autumn/fall.

quiz.q: "Tu la connais ?" means:
quiz.explanation: La is the feminine singular object pronoun, here referring to "her".

quiz.q: Futur proche is best used for:
quiz.explanation: The futur proche (aller + infinitive) expresses near or planned future actions, similar to English "going to".

grammar.title: Prepositions of place
grammar.explanation: À + definite article contracts: à + le → au, à + les → aux (à + la and à + l' stay the same). De behaves similarly: de + le → du, de + les → des.

examples.fr: C'est en face de la banque.

grammar.title: The imperative mood
grammar.explanation: Used for commands/instructions. Drop the subject pronoun and use the tu/nous/vous verb form (tu-form -er verbs drop the final -s: tourne, not tournes).

pronunciation.title: Open O (comme "porte") vs closed O (comme "beau")
pronunciation.tip: Closed o (as in beau, eau) is rounded and tense; open o (as in porte, votre) is more relaxed, closer to English "o" in "pot".

quiz.q: What does "à" + "le" contract to?
quiz.explanation: À + le always contracts to au.

quiz.q: Which command form correctly drops the -s from the tu form of an -er verb?
quiz.explanation: The imperative tu-form of -er verbs drops the final -s: Tourne à gauche.

quiz.q: "En face de la banque" means:
quiz.explanation: En face de means "across from/opposite".

quiz.q: Which contraction is correct for "de" + "les"?
quiz.explanation: De + les always contracts to des.

quiz.q: What does "le loyer" mean?
quiz.explanation: Le loyer means "the rent".

quiz.q: Imperatives are formed by:
options: Dropping the subject pronoun and using the verb form directly
quiz.explanation: French commands drop the subject pronoun and use the matching verb conjugation.

quiz.q: Which vowel sound is more relaxed/open?
quiz.explanation: The o in "porte" is the open variant, compared to the closed o in "beau".

quiz.q: "Près de" means:
quiz.explanation: Près de means "near/close to".

grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation: Comparative: plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que. Superlative: le/la/les plus/moins + adjective. Bon (good) is irregular: meilleur (better), le meilleur (best).

examples.fr: Elle est plus grande que moi.

grammar.title: Pouvoir, vouloir, devoir
grammar.explanation: These irregular modal verbs are followed directly by an infinitive: pouvoir (can/to be able to), vouloir (to want), devoir (must/to have to).

pronunciation.title: Word stress and rhythm
pronunciation.tip: French has no strong stressed syllable within a word like English does; stress falls lightly on the last syllable of a phrase/group, giving French its even, flowing rhythm.

examples.hint: even rhythm, slight emphasis only on the last syllable
flows as one smooth unit, no single stressed syllable

quiz.q: How do you say "taller than" using an adjective?
quiz.explanation: Plus + adjective + que forms the comparative "more ... than".

quiz.q: What is the irregular comparative of "bon"?
quiz.explanation: Bon has an irregular comparative form: meilleur.

quiz.q: "Je peux venir demain" means:
quiz.explanation: Pouvoir expresses ability/permission: "can".

quiz.q: Which verb expresses obligation?
quiz.explanation: Devoir means "must/to have to".

quiz.q: Where does French stress typically fall?
options: On the first syllable of every word
Lightly on the last syllable of a phrase
quiz.explanation: French stress is even, with a light emphasis on the final syllable of a phrase rather than a fixed word-stress like English.

quiz.q: "À mon avis" means:
quiz.explanation: À mon avis means "in my opinion".

quiz.q: What does "pire" mean?
quiz.explanation: Pire is the irregular comparative/superlative of mauvais, meaning "worse/worst".

quiz.q: Modal verbs like pouvoir, vouloir, devoir are followed by:
quiz.explanation: These modal verbs are directly followed by an infinitive, with no preposition needed.

units.title: Health, the body and il faut

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs in the passé composé
grammar.explanation: Reflexive verbs always use être in the passé composé, with the reflexive pronoun placed before être, and the participle usually agreeing with the subject.

grammar.title: Il faut + infinitive
grammar.explanation: Il faut is an impersonal expression meaning "it is necessary to / one must", followed directly by an infinitive. It never changes form for the subject.

pronunciation.title: The French CH sound
pronunciation.tip: French ch always makes a soft "sh" sound (as in English "shoe"), never a hard "ch" like in "chair".

examples.hint: shair-SHAY — both ch's are soft sh

quiz.q: Which auxiliary do reflexive verbs always use in the passé composé?
quiz.explanation: Reflexive verbs always take être as the auxiliary.

quiz.q: "Il faut boire de l'eau" means:
quiz.explanation: Il faut + infinitive expresses necessity: "one must/needs to".

quiz.q: How does "ch" sound in French?
quiz.explanation: French ch is consistently pronounced like the English "sh" sound.

quiz.q: What does "avoir mal à la tête" mean?
quiz.explanation: Avoir mal à + body part means "to have pain in...", here "headache".

quiz.q: Does "il faut" change form depending on who needs to do something?
options: Yes, it conjugates like a normal verb
quiz.explanation: Il faut is an impersonal expression and does not change for different subjects.

quiz.q: "Elle s'est levée tôt" — why does "levée" end in -ée?
options: Agreement with the feminine subject elle
All reflexive verbs end this way
quiz.explanation: With être (reflexive verbs), the participle agrees with the subject — feminine singular here.

quiz.q: What is "une pharmacie"?
quiz.explanation: Une pharmacie means "a pharmacy".

quiz.q: What does "guérir" mean?
quiz.explanation: Guérir means "to heal/recover".

grammar.title: Demonstrative adjectives and pronouns
grammar.explanation: Demonstrative adjectives (this/that): ce (masc.), cette (fem.), ces (plural), cet (before masc. vowel sound). Demonstrative pronouns (this one/that one): celui, celle, ceux, celles.

grammar.title: Introducing en and y
grammar.explanation: En replaces "de + noun" (often quantities); y replaces "à/en/dans + place". Both go right before the conjugated verb.

pronunciation.title: Distinguishing s (voiceless) vs z (voiced)
pronunciation.tip: A single s between vowels is pronounced z; a double ss stays as a hard s. Compare poison (poison, with z) and poisson (fish, with s).

quiz.q: Which demonstrative adjective goes with a masculine noun before a vowel sound?
quiz.explanation: Cet is used before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound, e.g. cet homme.

quiz.q: "J'en veux deux" means:
quiz.explanation: En replaces a quantity expression ("de + noun"): "two of them".

quiz.q: How is a single "s" between two vowels pronounced?
quiz.explanation: A lone intervocalic s is voiced, pronounced like "z": poison.

quiz.q: What does "en solde" mean?
quiz.explanation: En solde means "on sale".

quiz.q: "On y va ?" means:
quiz.explanation: Y replaces a previously mentioned place: "shall we go there?".

quiz.q: What is "la cabine d'essayage"?
quiz.explanation: La cabine d'essayage is the fitting room.

quiz.q: Which word means "to try on"?
quiz.explanation: Essayer means "to try/try on".

quiz.q: Demonstrative pronouns like celui/celle replace:
options: A noun already mentioned, meaning "this/that one"
quiz.explanation: Celui, celle, ceux, celles stand in for a noun to mean "this/that one(s)".

grammar.title: Mixed review: passé composé vs futur proche
grammar.explanation: Passé composé = completed past action (already happened). Futur proche (aller + infinitive) = near/planned future. Context words like "hier" (passé composé) or "demain" (futur proche) are strong clues.

examples.en: Yesterday, I ate at a restaurant.

examples.fr: Demain, je vais manger au restaurant.
examples.en: Tomorrow, I'm going to eat at a restaurant.

grammar.title: Object pronoun placement review
grammar.explanation: Direct (le/la/les), indirect (lui/leur) and adverbial (en/y) pronouns all go directly before the conjugated verb — or before the infinitive if there is one, when the pronoun's action belongs to that infinitive.

examples.en: I'm going to see him tomorrow.

pronunciation.title: Review: liaison, enchaînement, nasal vowels
pronunciation.tip: Before any listening test, warm up by reading a short paragraph aloud, paying attention to liaisons, smooth linking between words, and nasal vowels — don't let individual letters slow your flow.

quiz.q: Which tense fits "Hier, je ___ au cinéma"?
quiz.explanation: "Hier" signals a completed past action, requiring the passé composé: je suis allé(e).

quiz.q: Which tense fits "Demain, nous ___ voir un film"?
quiz.explanation: "Demain" signals the near future: nous allons voir un film.

quiz.q: In "Je vais le voir demain", where does the pronoun "le" sit?
options: At the very end of the sentence
quiz.explanation: When there's an infinitive, the object pronoun usually attaches just before that infinitive, not before the conjugated aller.

quiz.q: What does "réussir un examen" mean?
quiz.explanation: Réussir means "to succeed/pass".

quiz.q: "La compréhension orale" tests which skill?
quiz.explanation: Compréhension orale is listening comprehension.

quiz.q: Which word means "to fail"?
quiz.explanation: Échouer means "to fail".

quiz.q: Before a listening exam, a good warm-up is:
options: Reading a paragraph aloud, focused on liaison and linking
Avoiding any French the day before
quiz.explanation: Reading aloud with attention to liaison/linking trains your ear and mouth for natural spoken French.

quiz.q: "Les progrès" means:
quiz.explanation: Les progrès means "the progress".

grammar.title: Imparfait formation
grammar.explanation: Take the nous form of the present tense, drop -ons, and add: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Être is irregular: j'étais, tu étais, il était...

examples.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Lyon.
examples.en: When I was little, I lived in Lyon.
The weather was nice that day.

grammar.title: Imparfait vs passé composé
grammar.explanation: Imparfait describes background, ongoing states, habits or descriptions in the past (no clear end point). Passé composé describes specific completed events/actions.

examples.fr: Je lisais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.en: I was reading when the phone rang. (ongoing vs sudden event)

examples.fr: Chaque été, nous allions à la plage.
examples.en: Every summer, we used to go to the beach. (habit)

pronunciation.title: Imparfait endings: -ais, -ait, -aient all sound alike
pronunciation.tip: The je/tu/il/elle/ils/elles imparfait endings (-ais, -ait, -aient) are all pronounced identically — an open "eh" sound. Only nous/vous sound different (-ions/-iez).

examples.hint: both end in the same "eh" sound, spelling differs

quiz.q: Which tense describes an ongoing background state in the past?
quiz.explanation: Imparfait is used for descriptions, habits, and ongoing states without a clear endpoint.

quiz.q: "Je lisais quand le téléphone a sonné" — why is "a sonné" passé composé?
options: It's the sudden, specific event interrupting the background
All past tense must be passé composé
quiz.explanation: The phone ringing is a specific, completed event, contrasted with the ongoing imparfait action of reading.

quiz.q: What is the nous imparfait ending?
quiz.explanation: Nous takes -ions in the imparfait: nous parlions.

quiz.q: Do je, il/elle, and ils/elles imparfait endings sound different?
options: No, they all sound the same (open "eh")
quiz.explanation: -ais, -ait, and -aient are all pronounced identically despite different spelling.

quiz.q: "Chaque été, nous allions à la plage" expresses:
quiz.explanation: The imparfait with "chaque été" (every summer) expresses a repeated past habit.

quiz.q: What does "se souvenir de" mean?
quiz.explanation: Se souvenir de means "to remember".

quiz.q: Which irregular je-form is used for être in the imparfait?
quiz.explanation: Être's imparfait stem is ét-, giving j'étais.

quiz.q: "Soudain" means:
quiz.explanation: Soudain means "suddenly", often marking a shift to passé composé in a narrative.

units.title: Futur simple and real conditions (si + présent)

grammar.title: Futur simple
grammar.explanation: Formed from the infinitive (dropping final -e for -re verbs) + endings: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Several common verbs have irregular stems: être→ser-, avoir→aur-, faire→fer-, aller→ir-, pouvoir→pourr-.

examples.en: I will finish the project tomorrow.

grammar.title: Si-clauses, type 1 (real/likely condition)
grammar.explanation: For a realistic future condition: si + present tense in the "if" clause, futur simple in the result clause. Never use futur simple directly after si.

examples.en: If you study, you will succeed.

examples.fr: S'il fait beau, nous irons à la plage.
examples.en: If the weather is nice, we'll go to the beach.

pronunciation.title: The future-tense R cluster
pronunciation.tip: Futur simple endings add an r sound right after the infinitive stem (parlerai, finirai) — don't drop it, even though it can feel like a mouthful next to another consonant.

examples.hint: par-luh-RAY, the r is fully pronounced

quiz.q: What is the futur simple stem of "être"?
quiz.explanation: Être has the irregular futur simple stem ser-: je serai, tu seras...

quiz.q: Which tense follows "si" in a realistic future condition?
quiz.explanation: Si + présent, futur simple — never futur simple directly after si.

quiz.q: "Si tu étudies, tu réussiras" means:
options: If you studied, you would succeed
If you study, you will succeed
quiz.explanation: This is a type-1 si-clause: realistic present condition, future result.

quiz.q: What is the futur simple ending for "nous"?
quiz.explanation: Nous takes -ons in the futur simple, same ending shape as other tenses.

quiz.q: What does "durable" mean in an environmental context?
quiz.explanation: Durable means "sustainable" or "long-lasting".

quiz.q: Which verb means "to reduce"?
quiz.explanation: Réduire means "to reduce".

quiz.q: In futur simple, what do you add to an infinitive like "parler"?
quiz.explanation: Regular futur simple verbs keep the infinitive as the stem and simply add the endings.

quiz.q: "L'avenir" means:
quiz.explanation: L'avenir means "the future".

grammar.title: Conditionnel présent
grammar.explanation: Same stem as futur simple, but with imparfait endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Used for politeness, suggestions, and hypothetical results.

examples.fr: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

grammar.title: Si-clauses, type 2 (hypothetical/unreal condition)
grammar.explanation: For a hypothetical or unlikely present condition: si + imparfait in the "if" clause, conditionnel présent in the result clause.

examples.fr: Si j'avais plus de temps, je voyagerais plus.
examples.en: If I had more time, I would travel more.

examples.fr: Si elle était ici, elle nous aiderait.
examples.en: If she were here, she would help us.

pronunciation.title: Distinguishing futur simple vs conditionnel aurally
pronunciation.tip: Futur (je parlerai) and conditionnel (je parlerais) are spelled differently but sound almost identical in rapid speech — rely on context (a clear "if" clause signals conditionnel) more than ear alone.

examples.hint: par-luh-RAY in both cases, context distinguishes them
vyen-DRA / vyen-DRE, subtly different final vowel

quiz.q: What endings does the conditionnel présent use?
quiz.explanation: Conditionnel présent uses the futur stem with imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait...).

quiz.q: Which tense follows "si" in a hypothetical/unreal condition?
quiz.explanation: Si + imparfait, conditionnel présent — the type-2 si-clause pattern.

quiz.q: "Je voudrais un café" is more polite than "je veux un café" because:
quiz.explanation: Conditionnel is commonly used to make requests sound more polite/less direct.

quiz.q: "Si j'avais plus de temps, je voyagerais plus" means:
options: If I have more time, I will travel more
If I had more time, I would travel more
I had more time, so I travelled
I will have time to travel
quiz.explanation: Si + imparfait + conditionnel expresses a hypothetical present condition and its hypothetical result.

quiz.q: What does "à ta place" mean?
quiz.explanation: À ta place means "in your place/shoes", often introducing advice.

quiz.q: What does "malgré" mean?
quiz.explanation: Malgré means "despite".

quiz.q: Why can futur and conditionnel be hard to distinguish by ear?
options: They sound nearly identical in rapid speech
They are never used in the same context
quiz.explanation: The forms sound very close, so context (especially an "if" clause) is key to telling them apart.

quiz.q: Which word means "otherwise"?
quiz.explanation: Sinon means "otherwise".

grammar.title: Qui, que, où, dont
grammar.explanation: Qui = subject of the relative clause (who/which). Que = object of the relative clause (whom/which/that). Où = place/time (where/when). Dont = replaces "de + noun" (whose/of which).

examples.fr: L'homme qui parle est mon professeur.
examples.en: The man who is speaking is my teacher.

examples.fr: Le livre dont je parle est excellent.
examples.en: The book I'm talking about is excellent.

grammar.title: Joining ideas with relative clauses
grammar.explanation: Relative clauses let you combine two short sentences into one richer sentence, which is essential for B1-level writing and speaking fluency.

examples.fr: C'est la ville où j'ai grandi.
examples.en: It's the city where I grew up.

examples.fr: Voici le film que j'ai vu hier.
examples.en: Here's the film (that) I saw yesterday.

pronunciation.title: Reading longer sentences without pausing mid-clause
pronunciation.tip: French speakers group a sentence into short rhythmic units (groupes rythmiques) and pause between them, not mid-clause. Practise marking natural pause points before reading aloud.

examples.fr: L'homme qui parle / est mon professeur.
examples.hint: pause after the relative clause, not inside it

examples.fr: C'est la ville / où j'ai grandi.

quiz.q: Which relative pronoun is the SUBJECT of its clause?
quiz.explanation: Qui is used when the relative pronoun is the subject of the relative clause.

quiz.q: Which relative pronoun replaces "de + noun"?
quiz.explanation: Dont replaces a phrase built with de, e.g. "le livre dont je parle" (the book I'm talking about).

quiz.q: "Voici le film que j'ai vu hier" — why "que" and not "qui"?
options: Le film is the object of "j'ai vu", not the subject
Que is only used in questions
quiz.explanation: Que is used when the relative pronoun is the object of the clause — here, "le film" is what was seen.

quiz.q: "C'est la ville où j'ai grandi" uses "où" because it refers to:
quiz.explanation: Où is used for places (and sometimes time).

quiz.q: What does "selon" mean?
quiz.explanation: Selon means "according to".

quiz.q: What are "groupes rythmiques"?
options: Rhythmic word groups that French speech pauses between
quiz.explanation: Groupes rythmiques are the natural rhythmic chunks French sentences are spoken in, with pauses between them rather than within them.

quiz.q: What does "un reportage" mean?
quiz.explanation: Un reportage means "a news report".

quiz.q: Relative clauses are useful because they:
options: Combine two ideas into one richer sentence
Only work in the past tense
Replace the need for adjectives entirely
quiz.explanation: Relative clauses let you combine related ideas fluently into a single, more sophisticated sentence.

grammar.title: Introduction to the subjunctive
grammar.explanation: The subjunctive is used after expressions of necessity, desire, emotion or doubt, typically after "que". Formed from the ils present-tense stem + endings -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent (être and avoir are irregular).

examples.fr: Je veux que vous soyez à l'heure.
examples.en: I want you to be on time.

grammar.title: Common subjunctive triggers
grammar.explanation: Common phrases requiring the subjunctive: il faut que, vouloir que, il est important que, avoir peur que, être content(e) que, douter que.

examples.fr: Elle a peur qu'il soit en retard.
Nous sommes contents que tu sois là.

pronunciation.title: Emotional intonation
pronunciation.tip: French emotional speech relies more on intonation (pitch rising/falling across the sentence) than on stressing individual words — exaggerate the overall melody, not single syllables, to sound surprised, worried, etc.

examples.hint: rising pitch across the whole phrase for surprise

quiz.q: Which phrase requires the subjunctive?
quiz.explanation: Il faut que expresses necessity and triggers the subjunctive.

quiz.q: What stem is the regular subjunctive built from?
quiz.explanation: Regular subjunctive forms use the ils/elles present-tense stem plus subjunctive endings.

quiz.q: "Elle a peur qu'il soit en retard" means:
quiz.explanation: Avoir peur que triggers the subjunctive to express fear/worry about a possible event.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT typically trigger the subjunctive?
quiz.explanation: Je pense que expresses a belief/fact and is followed by the indicative, not the subjunctive.

quiz.q: What does "fier/fière" mean?
quiz.explanation: Fier/fière means "proud".

quiz.q: French emotional intonation relies mainly on:
options: Pitch rising and falling across the whole phrase
quiz.explanation: Overall melodic pitch contour across the phrase carries most of the emotional meaning in French.

quiz.q: What does "douter" mean?
quiz.explanation: Douter means "to doubt".

quiz.q: What does "défendre une idée" mean?
quiz.explanation: Défendre une idée means "to defend/argue for an idea", common in debates.

units.title: Pronoun mastery: en, y and double pronouns

grammar.title: En and y in depth
grammar.explanation: Y replaces à/dans/en/sur + a place or thing (penser à qqch → y penser). En replaces de + a thing, or expresses a quantity (avoir besoin de qqch → en avoir besoin).

examples.fr: Tu penses à ton travail ? — Oui, j'y pense.
examples.en: Are you thinking about your work? — Yes, I'm thinking about it.

examples.fr: Tu as besoin d'argent ? — Oui, j'en ai besoin.
examples.en: Do you need money? — Yes, I need (some).

grammar.title: Double object pronouns
grammar.explanation: When two pronouns combine, they follow a fixed order: me/te/se/nous/vous before le/la/les, which come before lui/leur, which come before y, which comes before en.

examples.en: She talks to them about it.

pronunciation.title: Speaking fluently with pronoun clusters
pronunciation.tip: Clusters like "il me le donne" or "elle leur en parle" should flow as one smooth breath group — practise them slowly first, then speed up, rather than pronouncing each pronoun separately.

quiz.q: What does "y" typically replace?
quiz.explanation: Y replaces locations or things introduced by à, dans, sur, en (location).

quiz.q: In "Il me le donne", what is the correct pronoun order rule?
quiz.explanation: Me/te/se/nous/vous come before le/la/les in the fixed pronoun order.

quiz.q: "J'en ai besoin" means:
quiz.explanation: En replaces "de + noun" after avoir besoin de, meaning "I need some/it".

quiz.q: What does "postuler" mean?
quiz.explanation: Postuler means "to apply (for a job)".

quiz.q: In the double-pronoun order, where does "y" sit relative to "en"?
quiz.explanation: The fixed order places y before en when both appear together.

quiz.q: What is "un logiciel"?
quiz.explanation: Un logiciel means "software".

quiz.q: How should pronoun clusters like "elle leur en parle" be practised aloud?
options: Each word separated by a pause
quiz.explanation: Pronoun clusters are spoken fluently as a single rhythmic unit in natural French.

quiz.q: What does "télécharger" mean?
quiz.explanation: Télécharger means "to download".

grammar.title: Plus-que-parfait (intro)
grammar.explanation: The plus-que-parfait (avoir/être in the imparfait + past participle) describes an action that happened before another past action — "had done" something.

examples.fr: Quand je suis arrivé, elle était déjà partie.
examples.en: When I arrived, she had already left.

examples.fr: Il avait déjà mangé quand nous sommes arrivés.
examples.en: He had already eaten when we arrived.

grammar.title: Logical connectors
grammar.explanation: Connectors make writing/speaking more sophisticated and are heavily tested at B1: donc (so/therefore), pourtant/cependant (however), parce que/car (because), bien que (although, + subjunctive), d'abord...ensuite...enfin (first...then...finally).

examples.fr: Il pleuvait, pourtant nous sommes sortis.
examples.en: It was raining, yet we went out.

examples.fr: Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il continue à travailler.
examples.en: Although he is tired, he keeps working.

pronunciation.title: Pacing a narrated story aloud
pronunciation.tip: When narrating, slow down slightly at connectors (d'abord, ensuite, enfin) — they act as verbal signposts for your listener, so give them a tiny beat of emphasis and a brief pause after.

quiz.q: The plus-que-parfait describes an action that:
quiz.explanation: Plus-que-parfait expresses "had done" something, before another past reference point.

quiz.q: "Elle était déjà partie" uses which auxiliary, and why?
options: Être, because partir is a être-verb
quiz.explanation: Partir takes être in compound tenses, including the plus-que-parfait.

quiz.q: Which connector means "although" and requires the subjunctive?
quiz.explanation: Bien que is a concession connector that triggers the subjunctive.

quiz.q: What does "par conséquent" mean?
quiz.explanation: Par conséquent means "consequently/as a result".

quiz.q: What does "entre-temps" mean?
quiz.explanation: Entre-temps means "meanwhile/in the meantime".

quiz.q: When narrating, what should you do at a connector like "ensuite"?
options: Give it a slight pause/beat as a verbal signpost
quiz.explanation: Connectors act as signposts in spoken narration and benefit from a small pause for clarity.

quiz.q: What is "un témoin"?
quiz.explanation: Un témoin means "a witness".

quiz.q: Which pair correctly orders a three-part narration?
quiz.explanation: D'abord (first), ensuite (then), enfin (finally) is the natural sequencing order.

grammar.title: Comparatives of equality and expressing nuance
grammar.explanation: Aussi...que (as...as) expresses equality; de plus en plus (more and more) and de moins en moins (less and less) express trends. These are common in opinion/debate writing.

examples.fr: Ce problème est aussi important que le changement climatique.
examples.en: This problem is as important as climate change.

examples.fr: De plus en plus de gens travaillent à distance.
examples.en: More and more people work remotely.

grammar.title: Subjunctive vs indicative recap
grammar.explanation: Use the indicative (present/futur/passé composé) after verbs of knowledge/certainty (savoir, être sûr que); use the subjunctive after verbs of doubt, emotion, necessity or desire — a core B1 distinction tested often.

vocab.en: on one hand... on the other hand...

pronunciation.title: Sounding persuasive: contrast stress
pronunciation.tip: In argumentation, a contrasting word (mais, cependant, en revanche) often gets a touch more emphasis and a brief pause before it, signalling the turn in your argument to the listener.

examples.fr: C'est vrai, / mais ça ne suffit pas.

examples.hint: clear separation between the two halves

quiz.q: "Aussi important que" expresses:
quiz.explanation: Aussi...que expresses equal comparison: "as...as".

quiz.q: Which verb phrase requires the indicative, not the subjunctive?
quiz.explanation: Être sûr que expresses certainty and takes the indicative.

quiz.q: "Je doute qu'il ait raison" — why "ait" instead of "a"?
options: Douter expresses doubt, triggering the subjunctive
quiz.explanation: Douter que triggers the subjunctive (ait, from avoir), expressing doubt rather than certainty.

quiz.q: What does "d'une part... d'autre part..." introduce?
options: Two contrasting sides of an argument
quiz.explanation: D'une part...d'autre part... presents two sides/aspects of an argument.

quiz.q: What does "convaincre" mean?
quiz.explanation: Convaincre means "to convince".

quiz.q: "De plus en plus" means:
quiz.explanation: De plus en plus means "more and more", describing an increasing trend.

quiz.q: In persuasive speech, a contrast word like "mais" often gets:
options: A slight pause and emphasis before it
quiz.explanation: A brief pause and lift before a contrast connector signals the argumentative turn to the listener.

quiz.q: What is "un inconvénient"?
quiz.explanation: Un inconvénient means "a disadvantage/drawback".

units.title: DELF A2 full review and mock exam

grammar.title: A2 grammar recap
grammar.explanation: Before the A2 checkpoint, make sure these are solid: être/avoir/aller/faire present, -er/-ir/-re regular verbs, passé composé (avoir and être), futur proche, possessives, object pronouns le/la/les, comparatives.

examples.fr: Nous sommes allés au marché et nous avons acheté du pain.
examples.en: We went to the market and bought bread.

examples.fr: Je vais appeler mon frère, il est plus jeune que moi.
examples.en: I'm going to call my brother, he's younger than me.

grammar.title: Exam technique: reading/listening comprehension
grammar.explanation: Skim the whole text/listen once for the general idea before hunting for details. Underline/note question keywords first, then search specifically for matching information rather than re-reading everything linearly.

examples.fr: Question : Où va-t-elle ? → cherchez un lieu dans le texte.
examples.en: Question: Where is she going? → scan the text specifically for a place.

pronunciation.title: Review: everything so far
pronunciation.tip: Record yourself reading a paragraph that mixes passé composé, futur proche and comparatives, then listen back for liaisons you missed and nasal vowels that sounded too English.

examples.fr: Nous sommes allés au marché et nous avons acheté du pain.
Il est plus jeune que moi.
examples.hint: check the open vs closed vowel in "jeune"

quiz.q: Before answering comprehension questions, you should first:
options: Skim/listen once for the general idea
Write your answers before reading the text
quiz.explanation: Getting the general idea first makes it much easier to locate specific details afterward.

quiz.q: Which verb combination is correctly conjugated in the passé composé?
quiz.explanation: Aller takes être, and the participle agrees with the plural subject nous: allés.

quiz.q: What does "cocher" mean in an exam context?
quiz.explanation: Cocher means "to tick/check a box", common in multiple-choice exam instructions.

quiz.q: "Il est plus jeune que moi" uses which structure?
quiz.explanation: Plus + adjective + que is the comparative of superiority ("more...than").

quiz.q: What does "gérer son temps" mean?
quiz.explanation: Gérer son temps means "to manage one's time", an important exam skill.

quiz.q: What is "le barème"?
quiz.explanation: Le barème is the grading scale showing how points are distributed.

quiz.q: Why re-listen/re-read after a first general pass?
options: To search specifically for details matching the questions
To change your initial answers randomly
quiz.explanation: A second, targeted pass helps you find specific details once you already know the general context.

quiz.q: What does "justifier" mean in an exam context?
options: To support an answer with evidence from the text
quiz.explanation: Justifier means to back up an answer with evidence, often required for true/false questions.

grammar.title: B1 grammar recap: tenses in combination
grammar.explanation: DELF B1 texts regularly mix imparfait, passé composé, futur simple and conditionnel in the same passage — practise identifying which tense is used and why (background vs event vs prediction vs hypothesis) rather than translating word by word.

examples.fr: Quand j'étais jeune, je ne savais pas que je deviendrais professeur.
examples.en: When I was young, I didn't know I would become a teacher.

examples.fr: S'il avait plus de budget, le projet réussirait.
examples.en: If it had more budget, the project would succeed.

grammar.title: Exam technique: longer listening passages
grammar.explanation: B1 listening often has two listens with increasing time pressure. On the first listen, note the topic, speakers and overall tone; on the second, fill in specific details (numbers, names, opinions) you missed.

examples.fr: Première écoute : sujet, locuteurs, ton général.
examples.en: First listen: topic, speakers, overall tone.

pronunciation.title: Tracking tense shifts by ear
pronunciation.tip: In fast native speech, imparfait/conditionnel and futur simple can be told apart partly by overall sentence melody and context words (quand, si, probablement) — train your ear on these cues rather than isolated verb endings.

examples.hint: "si" + imparfait cues a conditionnel result coming

quiz.q: "Je ne savais pas que je deviendrais professeur" mixes which two tenses?
quiz.explanation: Savais is imparfait (background state); deviendrais is conditionnel (what would happen from that past viewpoint).

quiz.q: On a two-listen B1 exam section, the first listen is mainly for:
options: Ignoring and waiting for the second listen
quiz.explanation: The first listen should establish the big picture before hunting for details on the second pass.

quiz.q: What does "déduire" mean?
quiz.explanation: Déduire means "to deduce/infer", a key skill for implicit exam questions.

quiz.q: What is "une consigne implicite"?
options: An instruction you must infer from context
quiz.explanation: An implicit instruction/requirement isn't stated outright and must be inferred from context.

quiz.q: "S'il avait plus de budget, le projet réussirait" is which type of si-clause?
quiz.explanation: Si + imparfait + conditionnel is the hypothetical/unreal present condition pattern.

quiz.q: What does "repérer" mean?
quiz.explanation: Repérer means "to spot/locate", useful when scanning for specific information.

quiz.q: What does "synthétiser" mean?
quiz.explanation: Synthétiser means "to summarise/synthesise" information.

quiz.q: Training your ear on words like "quand" and "si" helps you:
options: Anticipate which tense/structure is likely coming next
Avoid listening to the whole sentence
quiz.explanation: These cue words often signal a following tense pattern (quand+imparfait, si+imparfait/conditionnel, etc.).

grammar.title: Structuring a B1 opinion essay
grammar.explanation: A typical DELF B1 written production: intro (state the topic and your position), 2-3 body paragraphs each with one argument + an example, and a conclusion that restates your opinion. Use connectors (d'abord, de plus, cependant, en conclusion) to structure it clearly.

examples.fr: À mon avis, le télétravail présente plus d'avantages que d'inconvénients.
examples.en: In my opinion, remote work has more advantages than disadvantages.

grammar.title: Structuring a B1 spoken response
grammar.explanation: For the spoken monologue/debate section: state your position clearly and early, give 2 solid reasons with examples, acknowledge a counter-argument, then restate your position. Examiners reward structure and range of tenses, not just correctness.

examples.fr: Je suis plutôt favorable à cette idée, pour deux raisons.
examples.en: I'm rather in favour of this idea, for two reasons.

examples.fr: Certains diraient que..., mais je pense que...
examples.en: Some would say that..., but I think that...

vocab.en: to take care with one's speech

pronunciation.title: Fluency over perfection
pronunciation.tip: Examiners reward smooth delivery with occasional self-correction over hesitant, overly careful speech. If you make a mistake, rephrase briefly ("je veux dire...") and keep going rather than stopping.

examples.fr: Je pense... je veux dire, à mon avis...
examples.hint: a natural self-correction, not a full stop
a filler (enfin) buys thinking time without breaking flow

quiz.q: A B1 opinion essay should typically include:
options: Intro, body paragraphs with arguments/examples, and a conclusion
quiz.explanation: A clear structure with intro, developed body, and conclusion is expected at B1.

quiz.q: In the spoken section, examiners mainly reward:
options: Structure and range of tenses, not just correctness
quiz.explanation: Structure, coherence and range of language are valued alongside accuracy.

quiz.q: What does "reformuler" mean?
quiz.explanation: Reformuler means "to rephrase", a useful recovery strategy when you make a mistake.

quiz.q: "Certains diraient que..., mais je pense que..." demonstrates:
options: Acknowledging a counter-argument before restating your position
quiz.explanation: This structure shows awareness of other viewpoints while maintaining your own argument — valued at B1.

quiz.q: What is "le registre de langue"?
options: The level of formality in language
quiz.explanation: Le registre de langue refers to the level of formality (formal, informal, familiar) in speech or writing.

quiz.q: If you make a mistake while speaking, the best strategy is:
options: Stop completely and restart from the beginning
quiz.explanation: A brief self-correction keeps the flow going, which examiners generally reward over complete stops.

quiz.q: What does "un exemple concret" mean?
quiz.explanation: Un exemple concret means "a concrete/specific example", which strengthens an argument.

quiz.q: What does "l'aisance" mean in a speaking context?
quiz.explanation: L'aisance refers to fluency/ease of speech.

units.title: Final review and full mock exam

grammar.title: Full grammar recap: A1 through B1
grammar.explanation: Review, in order: être/avoir/aller/faire, regular -er/-ir/-re verbs, negation, possessives, passé composé (avoir & être), futur proche, imparfait, futur simple, conditionnel, relative pronouns (qui/que/où/dont), object pronouns (le/la/les/lui/leur/en/y), and the subjunctive after common triggers.

examples.fr: Si j'avais su que tu venais, j'aurais préparé un repas.
examples.en: If I had known you were coming, I would have prepared a meal.

examples.fr: Il faut que nous finissions avant qu'il ne parte.
examples.en: We need to finish before he leaves.

grammar.title: Final exam-day strategy
grammar.explanation: Across all four DELF skills: read every instruction twice, budget your time per section before starting, answer every question (an educated guess beats a blank), and leave a few minutes at the end to re-check grammar agreement (gender, number, tense) rather than content.

examples.fr: Vérifiez les accords (genre, nombre) à la fin.
examples.en: Check agreement (gender, number) at the end.

pronunciation.title: Final pronunciation self-check
pronunciation.tip: Record a two-minute monologue (e.g. describing your year of learning French) and check it against every pronunciation focus from this plan: nasal vowels, R, u vs ou, liaison/enchaînement, ch, rhythm, and intonation.

examples.hint: check liaison on "j'ai" and the nasal "an" in "année"

examples.fr: Je suis fier / fière de mes progrès.
examples.hint: check the French r and the vowel in "fier/fière"

quiz.q: "Si j'avais su que tu venais, j'aurais préparé un repas" uses which structure?
quiz.explanation: This is the third conditional pattern: si + plus-que-parfait, conditionnel passé — for an unreal past condition.

quiz.q: "Il faut que nous finissions" uses which mood, and why?
options: Subjunctive, because il faut que expresses necessity
quiz.explanation: Il faut que always triggers the subjunctive.

quiz.q: A good final exam-day strategy includes:
options: Budgeting time per section and answering every question
quiz.explanation: Time budgeting and attempting every question (educated guesses included) improve overall results.

quiz.q: What should you re-check in the last few minutes of a written exam?
options: Nothing, time is better spent elsewhere
quiz.explanation: A final pass focused on agreement errors (often the easiest to catch and fix) can meaningfully raise your score.

quiz.q: What does "consolider" mean?
quiz.explanation: Consolider means "to strengthen/consolidate" existing knowledge.

quiz.q: What does "persévérer" mean?
quiz.explanation: Persévérer means "to persevere", fitting advice at the end of a long learning plan.

quiz.q: Which object pronoun pair replaces "à quelqu'un" (indirect object, people)?
quiz.explanation: Lui (singular) and leur (plural) are the indirect object pronouns for people.

quiz.q: After finishing this plan, a realistic next step is to:
options: Take an official DELF A2/B1 exam and keep immersing yourself in French media
Only use the app, never speak to anyone
quiz.explanation: Sitting an official exam and continuing regular exposure (listening, reading, speaking) consolidates the level reached.
